arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Alan Beck argued for the sides that brought the case, per the Chief Justice's introduction of Case 24-1046. He urged reversal of the lower court's ruling upholding Hawaii's law.
Mr. Katyal argued for the state, defending the lower court's judgment in favor of Hawaii's consent requirement.

Ms. Harris argued for the sides that brought the case. She said analogs must be on all fours, and that inescapably different permissions govern property open to the public versus property closed to the public. She conceded this is not a complete answer to the state's position.

case.dek: Hawaii makes it a crime to carry a licensed firearm onto private property open to the public without the owner's express permission. Gun rights groups say the rule guts the constitutional right to public carry. The state says property owners' right to exclude controls. The Supreme Court heard the dispute in Wolford v. Lopez.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests how the Second Amendment right to carry firearms in public interacts with a property owner's traditional right to exclude people from private land. Hawaii's law requires express consent before a licensed carrier may bring a gun onto private property that is open to the public.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A lower court upheld Hawaii's law. the sides that brought the case asked the Supreme Court to reverse that decision and strike the rule down. The state asked the Court to affirm the lower ruling.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case: Alan Beck argued that Bruen protects the right to publicly carry firearms. He said Hawaii's consent requirement runs roughshod over that constitutional right.

the sides that brought the case: Ms. Harris contended that Hawaii cannot gut Bruen by presumptively banning licensed carriers from retail stores and other private property open to the public. She said the novel rule offends history and tradition, and that different common law traditions apply to property open to the public and property closed to it.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The state: Mr. Katyal argued the case involves two fundamental rights, the right to bear arms and the property right to exclude. He said the parties largely agree on how those rights interact.
Justice Thomas questioned the sides that brought the case' claim that the law blocks access to about 97 percent of public areas, asking how they arrived at that figure.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor pressed the sides that brought the case on whether the Constitution guarantees a right to carry a gun on private property.

Justice Sotomayor asked whether a custom permitting entry onto private property without the owner's express consent actually exists. She noted that under McKee, Justice Holmes looked for evidence that a practice prevailed in Missouri, the state where the suit originated. She said whether seashell collection was allowed depended on custom in that jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor also observed that much of Hawaii consists of state parks and state property. The Court's answer will shape whether states may condition gun carry on private land open to the public. Questions from the bench do not indicate votes.
